items.title: Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2, taking the #1 spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence ...
items.content:
Anthropic has released Claude Fable 5.2, taking the #1 spot on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 at 65, led by gains in science, knowledge, and coding

At max effort it scores 65, 5 points ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 60) and 6 ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 59). Gains are driven by scientific reasoning, knowledge and FrontierCode 2.0, and roughly matching Opus 5.5 on AA-Briefcase and Terminal-Bench 4.0.

Priced at $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens, a 20% reduction from Fable 5.1, Claude Fable 5.2 averages a Cost per Task of $26.5 with max effort, a ~2.6x increase compared to Opus 5.5 (max, $10.0) and ~2x compared to Fable 5.1 (max, $12.99)

Key takeaways:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 leads 5 of the 9 evaluations in the Intelligence Index: At max effort, Fable 5.2 scores 65, ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 60), Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 59) and GPT-6 Astra (max, 57), and ~15 points above Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 49). It sets the highest scores on HLE-Diamond (80%, previous best 69% from Gemini 4 Carbon), AA-Omniscience v1.1 (67, previous best 54 from Gemini 4 Carbon), Terminal-Bench-Science (73%, previous best 65% from Gemini 4 Carbon), CritPt v2 hard subset (77%, previous best 72% from GPT-6 Astra) and FrontierCode 2.0 (49%, previous best 46% from Claude Opus 5.5)

➤ Less progress in agentic knowledge work and terminal coding: Claude Fable 5.2 improves on Fable 5.1 across capabilities, but sometimes only to Opus 5.5 levels. It reaches 1785 Elo on AA-Briefcase, within the confidence interval of Opus 5.5 (1800) and just behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (1813). On GDP.pdf it reaches 24% all-pass against 26% for Opus 5.5. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scores 60%, level with Opus 5.5 and behind Kimi K3.1 Pro (67%), Gemini 4 Carbon (65%) and Sonnet 5.5 (64%). AutomationBench-AA is an exception, at 76% against 70% for Opus 5.5, narrowly behind Gemini 4 Carbon, 78%

➤ Lower efforts still take leading positions: With high and xhigh effort, Claude Fable 5.2 scores 62, ahead of every other model at any effort, using 98k output tokens per task against 173k for Opus 5.5 (max). At max effort Fable 5.2 costs ~2.6x more than Opus 5.5, but at lower effort settings it can outperform Opus 5.5 at lower cost per task

Other model details:

➤ Context window: 1 million tokens with image and text input

➤ Pricing: $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens; cache writes $10 with 5-minute TTL, $16 with 1-hour TTL, and cache reads $0.20

➤ Effort settings: five (low, medium, high, xhigh, max). Intelligence Index evaluations were run at all five with Anthropic's default fallback enabled

Congratulations to @AnthropicAI on this impressive release!

items.title: Meta's newest model Muse Ember scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Cla...
items.content:
Meta's newest model Muse Ember scores 36 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, matching Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at a third of the Cost per Task

Muse Ember is Meta's newest efficient-tier model line, with the same input and output token prices as Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna

Key Takeaways:

➤ On the Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task Pareto frontier at both max and xhigh effort. Muse Ember (max) is the cheapest model scoring 36 or higher, at $0.14 per task, and Muse Ember (xhigh) scores 34 for $0.12. Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) costs almost 3x more at $0.41 for the same score as Muse Ember (max). Muse Ember (max) is also about 4x cheaper than DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max, 33, $0.60) and GLM-5.3-Flash (28, $0.58)

➤ 8 points behind Muse Wonder for about 1/50th of the Cost per Task. Muse Wonder (max) scores 44 at $6.95 per Intelligence Index task

➤ Stands out on AutomationBench-AA. Muse Ember (max) scores 68.1% on AutomationBench-AA, level with Muse Wonder (max), and beats Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) on GDP.pdf (22.8% vs 20.8%), but trails it on AA-Briefcase (1521 vs 1574 Elo)

➤ Mixed in agentic coding in our Intelligence Index evaluations. It beats Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (40.9% vs 32.8%) but trails it on FrontierCode 2.0 (27.2% vs 34.9%)

➤ Ahead of similarly priced models when running in its own coding agent. In Muse Code, Muse Ember (max) scores 46 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, ahead of Claude Haiku 5.5 in Claude Code (max, 37) and GPT-6 Luna in Codex (max, 31)

➤ Knowledge is the main weakness, but it rarely hallucinates. Its AA-Omniscience accuracy of 21.1% is the lowest of the similarly intelligent models we compared, against 34.7% for Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) and 50.5% for Gemini 3.8 Flash (high). This is mostly because it declines to answer 64% of questions, which keeps its hallucination rate at 17.4%, half of Claude Haiku 5.5’s (max)

Other details:
➤ Pricing: $0.10 input / $0.004 cached input / $0.50 output per 1M tokens
➤ Reasoning effort: results shown at max effort, with xhigh also on the Intelligence vs. Cost chart ➤ Availability: Meta's first-party API and Muse Code

items.content:
The future of software

In the limit, of course, software won't mean anything anymore. Everything digital will be instantly created at will. But in the interim period we'll wander through an increasingly odd in-between age for software. This transition periodwill be defined by three new precepts.

Everflux software - instead of stepping from release to release, months apart, software now evolves continuously.

Software creation has broken the sound barrier of our own keystrokes, and every model release pushes it faster. There is no reason to wait weeks or months for the next release when a single company merges over 30,000 code changes a day. Cyber capabilities are also progressing at an increasing pace. Bug and vulnerability fixes need to ship quickly and continuously. And every piece of software sits in a lattice of dependencies, each one now shipping at a blistering pace. Software will have to move accordingly fast just to keep from breaking as everything around it shifts.

Translucent sources – A new territory has opened between open source and closed source.

Today Claude will happily pick apart any Electron app, and any binary shipped with debug symbols has become a reverse-engineering playground for LLMs. In other words, much so-called closed-source software is now open source in all but name, and keeping code closed makes less and less sense.

Even the notion of IP and copyright is breaking in software: Apps don't even need to be accessed to be reproduced. I'm writing this text on a personal text editor I prompted Claude to vibe-code from a few videos of people demoing editor features they liked. A mere description of the interface is increasingly enough for an LLM to rebuild the internals, whether or not they resemble the original. Software IP seems to be dissolving like cotton candy in a raccoon's paws.

Bespoke features - Now that all software is open source, nothing prevents us from modifying everything.

And personalization is just one prompt and a couple million tokens away, so there is absolutely no reason anymore to wait for someone else to add this feature you want. Everyone becomes their own product manager. Want a search box, an API bridge, a custom button? It's a couple of minutes away, mostly executed in the background of your daily life. Soon we'll want to personalize everything.

A major challenge appears when bespoke features crash into our first tenet: everflux software. How do you customize software without cutting yourself off from upstream? I could fork it for good to add my search box, but I'd lose all future benefit from the software creator, be it new security updates or other updates to the rest of the software. How do you personalize software that was never meant to be personalized, without shouldering all of its future maintenance?

Merge conflicts won't be the exception anymore; they'll be a constant of everflux software. Agents will rebase our personal features onto each new release overnight, and software will look less like a product and more like a living species, evolving through constant mutation.

Translucent sources – A new territory has opened between open source and closed source.

Today Claude will happily pick apart any Electron app, and any binary shipped with debug symbols has become a reverse-engineering playground for LLMs. In other words, much so-called closed-source software is now open source in all but name, and keeping code closed makes less and less sense.

Even the notion of IP and copyright is breaking in software: Apps don't even need to be accessed to be reproduced. I'm writing this text on a personal text editor I prompted Claude to vibe-code from a few videos of people demoing editor features they liked. A mere description of the interface is increasingly enough for an LLM to rebuild the internals, whether or not they resemble the original. Software IP seems to be dissolving like cotton candy in a raccoon's paws.

Bespoke features - Now that all software is open source, nothing prevents us from modifying everything.

And personalization is just one prompt and a couple million tokens away, so there is absolutely no reason anymore to wait for someone else to add this feature you want. Everyone becomes their own product manager. Want a search box, an API bridge, a custom button? It's a couple of minutes away, mostly executed in the background of your daily life. Soon we'll want to personalize everything.

A major challenge appears when bespoke features crash into our first tenet: everflux software. How do you customize software without cutting yourself off from upstream? I could fork it for good to add my search box, but I'd lose all future benefit from the software creator, be it new security updates or other updates to the rest of the software. How do you personalize software that was never meant to be personalized, without shouldering all of its future maintenance?

Merge conflicts won't be the exception anymore; they'll be a constant of everflux software. Agents will rebase our personal features onto each new release overnight, and software will look less like a product and more like a living species, evolving through constant mutation.

Image: M.C. Escher, Metamorphosis II, November 1939 - March 1940

items.title: Tempus AI CEO @lefkofsky reveals how its FDA-approved AI models can detect heart attack and stroke r...
items.content:
Tempus AI CEO @lefkofsky reveals how its FDA-approved AI models can detect heart attack and stroke risks that conventional ECG readings miss, and why general-purpose LLMs can't do the same:

"We have a large portfolio of ECG models that are FDA approved that look at a 12-lead ECG, the squiggly lines."

"About 3% of the time those squiggly lines are wrong. They tell you you're fine and you have a heart attack or stroke within a year. We have models that find that 3%."

"These LLMs weren't trained on that data, so they would just see squiggly lines. Or in the case of molecular data, if we just dump that data into a large language model, it would have no idea what it's reading."

"They weren't trained with clinical processes in mind, meaning you can't be right most of the time or almost all the time."

"You have to be right all the time or at least understand why you're coming up with the recommendation, so it can be unpacked by a physician."

"You just can't cheat the system because you've got human lives on the other side of this."
@TempusAI

items.content:
Last Thursday we hosted a private dinner for AI leaders in insurance at Niku Steakhouse.

The discussion was so good we forgot to take a photo :) We created a photorealistic rendering of what the conversation looked like below.

We live in a world where frontier models are exponentially improving every month. This raises many interesting questions around the opportunity for agentic automation, both within the external products that folks are building (e.g. automating claims, underwriting), and within internal organization and engineering processes.

We opened with two questions:
1. How much of your work is AI actually automating today?
2. In an industry this regulated, where does a human stay in the loop?

Human in the loop will always be needed for verification and legal purposes in highly regulated environments. But it is fascinating to see that most builders have evolved from building small deterministic workflows into agents that can deliver e2e outcomes. They're also able to build product with a team that's leaner than ever and still multiples more productive than the same time last year.

Big thanks to @imaanxsultan for organizing! 

This is the first dinner for Marginalia, a private dinner series that gathers AI leaders one industry at a time. Thanks to everyone for a great discussion, and we’re hoping to host the next one soon!

Yes, we'll have way more slop going around, but the market will pick winners and losers like it always does.

So, while right now this will be a problem for indie hackers and small software builders, it will end up being great for the industry overall.
